content: Silent thyroiditis, also referred to as subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis, is a form of resolving thyroiditis that includes postpartum thyroiditis. It was initially described as a painless variant of subacute thyroiditis due to its similar clinical course. However, it is distinguished from postpartum thyroiditis by its occurrence outside the postpartum period. The exact mechanism underlying silent thyroiditis remains unclear, but it is believed to be an autoimmune condition. Patients with silent thyroiditis exhibit elevated levels of activated T-cells, including matured T-cells (HLA-DR+CD3+), helper/inducer T-cells (HLA-DR+CD4+), and cytotoxic T-cells (HLA-DR+CD8+), compared to healthy individuals. This suggests that T-cell activation, particularly of helper/inducer T-cells, plays a significant role in its pathogenesis. The condition is associated with the HLA-DR3 and DR5 genes. Histological findings include lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, with an absence of Hurthle cells and germinal centers. Silent thyroiditis may result from the activation of helper and cytotoxic T-cells, genetic predisposition, and autoimmune antibodies. It is a rare condition, with an incidence of up to 23,000 cases per 100,000 individuals with hyperthyroidism and a prevalence of approximately 1,000 cases per 100,000 individuals with thyrotoxicosis. It most commonly affects individuals aged 30 to 40 years, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 4:1. The condition is more prevalent in regions with higher dietary iodine intake. Risk factors include the use of lithium, radiation therapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma, cessation of corticosteroids in Cushing's syndrome (post-adrenalectomy), and certain autoimmune disorders. Silent thyroiditis typically presents with symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, such as palpitations, tachycardia, nervousness, and tremors. The disease progresses through a euthyroid phase and may lead to a hypothyroid phase before resolving completely. Complications can include hypothyroidism. There are no established diagnostic criteria for silent thyroiditis, but decreased radioactive iodine uptake and elevated serum T3 and T4 levels are useful diagnostic indicators. Histopathological analysis is essential to differentiate silent thyroiditis from other forms of thyroiditis. Patients often report fatigue and restlessness and may have a history of other autoimmune diseases, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), or lymphocytic hypophysitis. On physical examination, tachycardia and palpitations are common findings. During the recovery phase, signs of hypothyroidism may become apparent. Laboratory findings in the thyrotoxic phase typically include elevated free T3 and T4 levels with decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), while the hypothyroid phase shows decreased free T3 and T4 with increased TSH. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are often elevated. Electrocardiogram (EKG) findings in thyrotoxicosis commonly reveal sinus tachycardia, though rare cases may show myocardial damage, including ST-segment elevation and arrhythmias. Imaging studies are not routinely used for diagnosis. Ultrasound findings may include hypoechoic areas, glandular irregularities, and a nonhomogeneous echotexture. Diffusion-weighted MRI may show a low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), and 24-hour iodine-123 uptake is typically decreased. Histological analysis may reveal inflammatory cell infiltration, lymphoid follicles, and loss of follicular integrity. Fine-needle aspiration cytology can help distinguish between benign and malignant thyroid nodules. Treatment for silent thyroiditis is primarily medical. Beta-blockers are used to manage symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, while levothyroxine may be prescribed for hypothyroidism if it follows the hyperthyroid phase. Surgical intervention is rarely indicated and is reserved for cases with repeated relapses despite appropriate treatment.
